One record, every pharmacy

Designing IMS — the system that ends 1-drug-equals-8-records, and becomes the single source of truth that Provider Web, the patient app, Plato, and OMS all read from.

400+SKUs currently living in Edward's head

Q3 2026Phase 1 · in engineering build
01 — Problem statement

A warehouse run from one person's memory

Doctor Anywhere runs medication like a hub-and-spoke network: Marina Health is the central warehouse, feeding stock out to 13 locations — 8 pharmacies, medsuites, and the PFC. That network is coordinated today by four systems that have never spoken to each other: an Excel masterlist, AP1 (prescribing config), Plato (fulfilment stock), and NetSuite (finance, out of scope here). None of them share a key. Every one of them needs a human to keep them in sync.

That human is Edward Tan. Every Friday he reviews the week's clinical usage, decides what to add, deactivate, or reprice — then opens AP1 and repeats the same edit eight times, once per pharmacy, because AP1 has no concept of "one drug." There is no audit trail if a number slips. There is no way for anyone else to check his work, because the configuration logic isn't written down anywhere except in his head.

1 new drug activation = 8 separate records in AP1, 1 Excel update, 1 Plato entry. Any price change = 8 manual edits. No audit trail anywhere. All config knowledge lives in one person's head.Research overview — core problem statement

IMS's entire premise follows from that: one ITEM_MASTER record per drug, referenced — never copied — by every pharmacy, pricing scheme, and prescribing surface. Edit once, and Provider Web, the patient app, Plato, and OMS all see it the same instant. Excel and AP1 retire.

02 — My role, and why this follows OMS

The same designer, a longer runway

I own IMS the same way I own OMS — end to end, from the first shadowing session at Marina Health through to the module designs shipping into engineering now. The difference is sequencing, not ownership: OMS shipped first because its scope could be isolated to one team and one event contract; IMS had to retire four systems across two teams before it could ship anything at all.

That's why IMS reads less like a trial-and-fix story and more like an information-architecture one. The research discipline is the same — shadowing, stakeholder interviews, a design audit — applied to a much wider blast radius: 13 locations, two teams, and a data model everything downstream depends on.

03 — Field research

Shadowing the four systems in the wild

Before a single screen, the work was to see the mess first-hand — shadowing Edward's Friday cycle, photographing the Marina Health warehouse, capturing AP1 and Plato mid-use, and transcribing it all into notebook flows. This is the raw observation board: real screens, real shelves, real handwriting.

05 — Who IMS has to satisfy

Three people, three very different relationships to the same record

IMS has exactly one data model but three audiences who touch it differently: one who configures everything, one who has to trust what's configured before it reaches patients, and one who mostly just needs to know it isn't broken.

Marina Health Config Admin
Edward Tan
"Create or update a medication once — it propagates everywhere, without me doing it 8 times."
  • 1 drug = 8 AP1 records to edit
  • No audit trail if something breaks
  • All config knowledge is in his head alone
Solved: one record, one edit, full audit trail, one-click deactivate.
PFC Ops Lead
Peiyi Lim
"Receive stock with batch/expiry captured once — no daily reconciliation between Plato's FIFO and my physical FEFO."
  • Plato deducts FIFO, she dispenses FEFO — daily mismatch
  • Edward's new items go live with no PFC review
  • Errors surface only at audit, weeks later
Solved: deliberate activation she can review first. FEFO deduction is Phase 1B.
Clinic Admin
Sarah Ng
"See what we have and what's arriving, without chasing Marina Health."
  • No consolidated view of clinic stock
  • Reconstructs status from Plato adjustment logs
  • Can't tell pending, deactivated, or never-created apart
Solved: formulary status visible read-only. Real-time stock is Phase 1B.

07 — A scaling problem, solved on the page

What happens when "pharmacy" stops meaning 9

The very first pharmacy-availability design used a dot matrix of 9 fixed entities — fine when Marina Health, PFC, and a handful of clinics were the whole network. Then the real number arrived: up to 50 pharmacies. The 9-dot pattern couldn't scale, and neither could its first replacement.

Broke at 50

Inline chips + search

Fine for 5–10 selections. At 50, chips wrap uncontrollably, there's no bulk selection, and no way to group by region.

Corporate VC DASG × Cigna VC DASG × Income VC DASG × HSBC VC DASG × Cigna Secure Plan × AXA Shield Plus × Prudential Care Elite × Manulife Flex × … ×47 more
Holds at 50

3-radio + selector panel

All pharmacies · Include specific · Exclude specific — with a region-grouped panel, bulk "select all in region," and a live count.

● Include specific pharmacies [ Edit selection ] 23 pharmacies selected ▾ SG (18): Marina Health · Clinic Full · +16 ▾ MY (5): Petaling Jaya · TTDI · +3 more

The insight that survived: keeping Exclude as a first-class option, not just Include. If a drug is available at 48 of 50 pharmacies, excluding 2 is a far shorter interaction than including 48 — the interface should let the admin pick whichever direction requires fewer clicks.

Still open: whether availability stays 3-state (Ex-stock / Special order / N/A) per pharmacy at this scale, and what happens to an item marked "All pharmacies" when a 51st pharmacy is added later.

09 — Decisions worth knowing

A few calls that shaped the model

Audit architecture
The audit log lives on the item, not the module
Pricing Scheme and Pharmacy each keep their own module-level log, but every change touching a specific item — pricing, availability, status, clinical details — also lands on that item's own Audit log tab. Edward should open one drug and see its entire history without checking three places.
Bulk vs. individual
Not every audit entry should read the same way
A single edit shows inline before/after. A bulk UI action shows a count plus an expandable list. A CSV upload shows the filename, processed/updated/failed counts, and a downloadable error file — never a flood of individual row entries. Three shapes for three different actions.
Templates
Deactivate, not delete
An earlier draft modal used permanent-delete language. Templates carry operational history — deleting one destroys auditability that regulated medication data shouldn't lose. Awaiting PM confirmation before engineering builds the delete flow.
Pricing scheme creation
Clone is mandatory, not optional — a real bug caught in review
The PRD requires every new pricing scheme to clone from an existing one; the Figma modal showed cloning as optional with "leave blank to start with empty prices." An empty scheme should never be creatable. Fix: remove the blank-state copy and enforce the clone step.
10 — Business impact

What one record actually buys

Translated out of UX metrics: IMS turns a single person's Friday afternoon into infrastructure. Every pharmacy DA opens, every price change a scheme owner makes, and every SKU Edward retires stops being a manual multi-system sweep and becomes one auditable edit — the same edit whether it's pharmacy 1 or pharmacy 50.

8→1edits per price change — the ceiling on how fast Marina Health can react to a formulary decision, removed
13locations IMS can onboard without adding linear admin overhead per pharmacy
1person no longer a single point of failure for 400+ SKUs of clinical and pricing data
0→1audit trails — from none, across 4 systems, to one, on every item

IMS is now in engineering build, not live yet — so this is the value the design is built to unlock, traced line for line back to the pain points in the coverage scoreboard above, not a hypothetical.
